1.pericope_label: And Job answered and said, No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you. But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these? I am as one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth upon God, and he answereth him: the just upright man is laughed to scorn. He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease. The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure; into whose hand God bringeth abundantly.

schools.summary: Ellicott narrows the mocking verse to one question, whether this is the character Job claims or the supposed taunt of his friends, and adds that ridicule is no test of truth or of merit; on the lamp he says the English rendering conveys no sense and offers two constructions, preferring the one that makes contempt for calamity lie ready in the thoughts of the man at ease.

Gill reaches the ironic reading by eliminating the alternative, that the friends were merely of the common people, since Job goes on to compare himself with them; he notes the marginal reading that Job has a heart as well as they, and records an alternative from Sephorno on the mocking before preferring to read Job as instancing himself as proof that good men are afflicted.

Clarke calls the opening a strong irony, turns the counter-claim against the friends by saying their boasted wisdom is only strings of proverbs in every person's mouth, declares the mocking verse very difficult with no two critics agreed and lays three renderings side by side, and refuses the inference from the prosperity of robbers, that providence cannot be accounted for yet the Judge of all the earth does right; Wesley makes the same evenness, that neither side has reason to be puffed up since the most barbarous nations know God to be infinite in wisdom, but that this is not the question between them.

Henry hears a claim to the monopoly of wisdom and thinks Job may be turning back Zophar's comparison of him to the wild ass's colt, reads the counter-claim as said to humble the friends rather than to magnify Job, alone doubts that the friends meant any mockery, and supplies the image of a lamp taken out of its golden candlestick and put into an earthen pitcher.

debates: Whether the opening grants the friends any standing, where Gill weighs the sense that they are merely common people against the ironic sense and settles on irony because Job compares himself with them.

What the fourth verse means, which Clarke calls very difficult with no two critics agreed, setting Good, Coverdale and Parkhurst side by side, while Ellicott reduces the question to whether Job claims the character or quotes the taunt.

What the lamp of the fifth verse is, where Ellicott rejects the English rendering outright and chooses between a torch disregarded by those at ease and contempt for calamity lying ready in their thoughts.
outliers: Henry and Wesley draw the same consolation in almost the same words, that wisdom and goodness do not die with wise and good men, since God has the residue of the Spirit and can raise up others more fit to do his work.
Clarke ends his survey of the renderings by observing that to emendations and conjectures there is no end.
themes: And Job answered and said,
No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you.
But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these?
I am as one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth upon God, and he answereth him: the just upright man is laughed to scorn.
He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease.
The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure; into whose hand God bringeth abundantly.

7.pericope_label: But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the Lord hath wrought this? In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind. Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat? With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that this is the only place in the dialogue parts of the book where the sacred name appears and that no friend ever uses it, making Job's use of it evidence of the superior knowledge he claims; on the ear and palate he makes Bildad the target and turns the concession about age by remarking that the Ancient of Days must needs be wise indeed. Delitzsch states the rule flatly, that the sayings of the ancients are not to be accepted without being proved.

Gill makes the lesson of the beasts a hard one and specifies it, that the harmless and useful creatures are the ones that fall prey and that the profitable creatures fall more to the wicked than the good, so that nature itself shows the righteous afflicted; he adds the vegetable witness, keeps the tenth verse providential with the sparrow not worth a farthing, and canvasses four readings of the wisdom of the ancients before settling on a proverb.

Clarke gives most of his space to Good's paraphrase, that this is the common doctrine of all nature but that to infer hypocrisy from it is impertinent, works on the two Hebrew terms for soul and breath, dismisses the friends' sayings as common-place that cast no light on providence, and supplies a historical reason for the wisdom of the ancients in the recentness of the great facts; Wesley reads the appeal to the beasts as a rebuke of method, notes that God was then more known by the name Shaddai, takes the ear and palate as a preface inviting candid judgment, and attaches to the concession about antiquity the reservation that such wisdom is imperfect.

debates: What the beasts are being asked to teach: that God is universal creator and controller, as Good's paraphrase has it, or that nature itself exhibits the harmless as prey and the profitable in wicked hands, as Gill reads it.

Whom the rule of the ear and the palate is aimed at, where Ellicott makes it Bildad and his appeal to tradition, Clarke the friends in general for advancing nothing new, and Wesley neither, taking it as a preface inviting candid judgment.

What is meant by wisdom being with the ancient, where Gill canvasses four readings and prefers a proverb, Clarke grounds it in the recentness of the great facts of nature, and Wesley concedes it only with the reservation that antiquity is not to be received against the truths of God.
outliers: Ellicott and Wesley independently notice that the covenant name occurs here and nowhere else in the discourses, Wesley adding that God was then more commonly known as Shaddai, the Almighty.
themes: But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee:
Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee.
Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the Lord hath wrought this?
In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind.
Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?
With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding.

13.pericope_label: With him is wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding. Behold, he breaketh down, and it cannot be built again: he shutteth up a man, and there can be no opening. Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth. With him is strength and wisdom: the deceived and the deceiver are his. He leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools. He looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle. He leadeth princes away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty.

schools.summary: Ellicott compresses the breaking down into a sentence, that God has equal power over the moral and the physical world, makes the loosed bond the confederacy by which kings bind themselves together, judges that the parallelism of the nineteenth verse suits princes better than priests, and reads the passage as re-echoing Eliphaz while refusing his optimism, since Eliphaz generalises vaguely where Job declares that not men but nations are the subjects of God's providence.

Gill registers the repetition without pressing it, works at identifying what was broken down and prefers Sodom with Sephorno over the tower of Babel, keeps three senses of the waters open including the drying of the brook Cherith, makes the deep things the decrees and thoughts of God hid until their accomplishment, offers two senses of the loosing of the bond, and reports the Greek rendering that leads the priests away captive.

Clarke denies that the opening and closing formulas are the same, the first pairing intelligence with fortitude or strength in action and the second strength with sufficiency or power in essence, and concludes that with God is every excellence in potentia and in esse; he argues the breaking down from physics before history, that nothing can be annihilated but by the power that made it, names the cities broken down never to be rebuilt, hears the creation and the flood together in the waters, and reports the reading that refers the deceiver to the fall; Wesley gives the repeated formula a function, reads the waters of the clouds and the rivers, explains the girding from the custom of servants, and guards the doctrine by saying God governs the deceiver without being the author of any error or sin.

debates: Whether the formula that opens and closes the hymn is a simple repetition, as Gill and Wesley take it, or two distinct assertions, as Clarke argues from the different Hebrew pairs.

What the deep things brought out of darkness are: the decrees and thoughts of God hid until their accomplishment (Gill), or God's works in the great deep, or the conspiracies of wicked men about to be exposed (both Clarke).
Whether the nineteenth verse speaks of princes or of priests, where Gill reports the Greek rendering for priests and Ellicott judges the parallelism to favour princes.
outliers: Clarke argues the breaking down from the impossibility of annihilation, that man may change the form of matter by chemical agency but to reduce it to nothing belongs to God alone.

Wesley states the guard the clause about the deceiver needs, that God governs the deceiver and sets bounds to his deceits yet is not the author of any error or sin but only the wise and holy governor of it.
themes: With him is wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding.
Behold, he breaketh down, and it cannot be built again: he shutteth up a man, and there can be no opening.
Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth.
With him is strength and wisdom: the deceived and the deceiver are his.
He leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools.
He looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle.
He leadeth princes away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty.

20.pericope_label: He removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the understanding of the aged. He poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty. He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death. He increaseth the nations, and destroyeth them: he enlargeth the nations, and straiteneth them again. He taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilderness where there is no way. They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the passage the key to much of the history of the world, framing it as two questions about the characteristic differences of nations and the failure of the wisest counsel, answers that One is working underneath it all, measures Zophar against Job on whether the dealings of God are intelligible or inscrutable, concedes that Job's teaching may seem to savour of fatalism while insisting he would have stated man's responsibility with equal force, and concludes that Job is just in saying he is not inferior to his friends.

Gill takes the removal of speech as the withdrawal of a gift and lists the ways, at death, by striking dumb, by confusion at Babel and by constraint as in Balaam; he spends his space on the princes who are not meant before naming those who are, makes the deep things the thoughts and decrees of God hid until their accomplishment, and assembles a history of nations increased and destroyed from the flood through the seven nations of Canaan to the four monarchies.

Clarke quotes the tag that God infatuates those whom he is determined to destroy and compares the helpless elders to a child who can neither reason nor speak, parses the word for princes as those of royal extraction and the weakening of the mighty as the loosing of a girdle, ventures from there a reference to the crocodile and its armour of fifty-two girdles of square scales, offers two senses of the deep things, and follows Good in rendering that God lets the nations grow licentious, with luxury and profligacy bringing on a less pampered conqueror.

debates: What the deep things brought out of darkness are, where Gill makes them the hidden decrees of God and Clarke offers instead God's works in the great deep or the conspiracies of wicked men on the point of exposure.
What the increase of the nations means, where Gill reads a plain history of peoples multiplied and destroyed while Clarke follows Good in making the verb mean that God lets them grow licentious.
Whether the chapter's doctrine savours of fatalism, which Ellicott concedes it may seem to do and answers by saying Job deals with one side of the problem only.
outliers: Clarke moves from the loosing of a girdle to the crocodile, setting out its fifty-two parallel girdles of square scales and asking what human strength is against it, since God alone can loose the girdles of that mighty one.
themes: He removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the understanding of the aged.
He poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty.
He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death.
He increaseth the nations, and destroyeth them: he enlargeth the nations, and straiteneth them again.
He taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilderness where there is no way.
They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like a drunken man.
